sections.skill: Tell recorded events from predictions and judge capability claims

questions.domain: Society: history and claims about the future
questions.prompt: In this fictional headline, which part is a recorded event?
questions.intro: Headlines about AI mix RECORDED EVENTS ("a model was released on March 3"), CAPABILITY CLAIMS ("it solves difficult math problems") and PREDICTIONS ("AI will replace most jobs by 2030"). Each needs different checking. Events can be confirmed from records. Capability claims need EVIDENCE: what tests, how many, who ran them, compared with what? Predictions are uncertain by nature; check who is predicting, their track record, and what assumptions they make. A confident tone does not turn a prediction into a fact.

sections.skill: Sort headline statements into three kinds

questions.domain: Society: history and claims about the future
questions.prompt: "Launched last week" is which kind?
questions.intro: Sort each statement. RECORDED EVENT: something that happened, checkable in records ("signed on May 1"). CAPABILITY CLAIM: what a system can do, which needs test evidence ("translates 100 languages"). PREDICTION: what will happen ("will cure diseases within five years"). Example: "Launched last week, the app detects skin cancer as well as doctors and will save millions of lives." Event: launched last week. Capability: detects as well as doctors. Prediction: will save millions.

sections.skill: Use history for perspective on predictions

questions.domain: Society: history and claims about the future
questions.prompt: Have AI predictions historically been wrong?

choices.text: No, every prediction about AI has come true exactly on the date that was predicted

questions.intro: History offers perspective: confident predictions about AI have been wrong in both directions, too early and too late. Demos may show the best attempt out of many. Press releases may omit failures. Independent checks, such as other researchers repeating a test, strengthen a claim. When reading a headline, find the original source, separate the three kinds of statements, and give each the trust its evidence earns.
